content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper presents a policy learning algorithm from logged data with known propensity and both known and unknown rewards.
It frames the problem as a standard counterfactual risk minimization (CRM) problem, regularized using the observations with unknown rewards.
The authors justify the approach providing an upper bound on the variance of the inverse propensity score that depends on the KL-divergence (or reverse KL) between the target policy and the logging policy.
Three algorithms, with small variations of the framework described above, are provided and tested on synthetically built example, transforming supervised tasks into logged bandit feedback tasks. Comparison with state-of-the-art (which do not include regularization for observations with unknown rewards) show stark improvements in terms of expected risk and accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is solid, from both the theoretical perspective and the algorithmic perspective. Due to time constrains

The only open question that I have is on the choice of computing the regularization term only on the observations with unknown rewards (see eq. 10 and 11)? Would it be beneficial to include all the observations in the regularization term? Could we use the regularization term to bound the variance also in the case of observations with only known-rewards?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clear in all its parts. To the knowledge of the reviewer the work is novel in the field of counterfactual risk minimization. It has overlap with semi-supervised learning settings, which are correctly mentioned in the "related works" section (and appendix).
Code is provided with notebooks to reproduce the presented results.
content.summary_of_the_review: I recommend the acceptance of the paper, due to the novelty of the work and correctness of its content.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose three approaches for neural semi-CRM, two based upon KL-divergences between the learned policy and the logging policy on the unknown reward set, termed KL-CRM and WCE-CRM, and the third based upon a extension of WCE-CRM and the truncated IPS approach based upon estimated rewards. Empirical comparisons on Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets using the VGG-16 architecture demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approaches.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

1.
The paper is theoretically well-motivated. In particular, the regularizers in the proposed WCE-CRM and KL-CRM approaches are nicely motivated by the bound in Theorem 1.

2.
Ancillary propositions 2 and 3 further buttress the empirical procedure used to estimate the KL-divergence used in either algorithm.

Weaknesses

1.
Unlike the WCE-CRM and KL-CRM approaches, the pseudo reward PR-CRM approach is not purely motivated by the generalization bound in Theorem 1. It performs slightly worse than the WCE-CRM approach although it includes the WCE term. It appears as if pseudo-reward estimation provides no additional value. But no discussion is provided for this observation in the paper.

2.
The "two terms" explanation for why KL-CRM underperforms w.r.t. WCE-CRM in terms of test set accuracy and risk seems rather cryptic to this reviewer.

3.
Typos exist, e.g., Joachim's 2018 BanditNet approach is referred to as "BandiNet" in the paper.

4.
The empirical evaluation demonstrates advantages over BanditNet when the known reward set size is set to 10% of the total set.
Ideally, experiments should be conducted where this percentage is increased. In the advertising example mentioned in the introduction, it is quite unlikely that known reward examples would form only 10% of the total set since advertisers can only be charged in CPC (cost-per-click) auctions when the reward is known.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is generally clear, but certain choices are not well-motivated.
The theoretical bound in Theorem 1 suggests the use of both the forward and reverse KL-divergences. But the algorithms only use one of the two divergences at a time.
Additionally, either KL divergence could be estimated using both labeled (known reward) and unlabeled samples, but only unknown-reward samples are used. The motivation for this choice is not clarified.

The quality of the theoretical work appears to be quite high, but the experimental section could be strengthened as discussed in the weaknesses above.

The novelty does not appear to be extremely high as regularizers because upon KL-divergence are quite common in the literature for different problems. However, the theoretical bound in theorem 1 provides a strong justification for their usage in this problem.

With regard to reproducibility, enough details are generally provided and the code is provided in the supplementary material. 
However, it is not clear from the description how the parameters m_1 and n_1 in Algorithm 1 were set.
content.summary_of_the_review: This reviewer has certain relatively minor concerns with regard to clarity and the empirical evaluation as detailed above. However, the paper appears to be theoretically strong and sufficiently novel. Hence I recommend acceptance.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
-Studies counterfactual risk minimization under missing rewards. 

-Provides new KL and Reverse KL-based upper bounds on the true risk for the IPS estimator.

-Provides consistent and unbiased estimator of KL and Reverse KL divergences for logged unknown-reward datasets. 

-Proposes a pseudo-labeling-like approach to produce pseudo-rewards for the logged unknown-reward dataset from a logged known-reward dataset. Therefore, the IPS estimator can be applied to logged unknown-reward dataset after filling in pseudo-rewards.  

-Experiments are performed to evaluate the usage of the unknown-reward dataset to improve over baseline methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
-Missing rewards are ubiquitous in advertising and healthcare. Current work tries to address this critical issue. 

-The paper provides novel methods for CRM when both logged known-reward, and unknown-reward datasets are available. Experiments show improvements over baseline methods.

Weaknesses: 

-Theoretical contributions are somewhat incremental. 

-The paper is dedicated to showing results for loss functions based on the IPS estimator (with truncated propensity scores). It is discussed by the authors that many importance weighting scores are considered in prior works. It is not clear why the IPS estimator with truncated propensity scores is chosen for Semi Counterfactual Risk Minimization (CRM). Is this really the best approach for tackling Semi CRM? More comparisons with state-of-the-art in experiments will be necessary to understand how well the proposed methods perform. 

-Can the dependence of the upper bound in Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 on $w_m$ be improved, or is this dependence optimal? The upper bound will be very loose for policies that significantly differ from the logging policy in terms of action probabilities. 

-Proposition 1 improves upon the chi-square divergence-based bound of Cortes et al. 2010 on the variance of the importance-weighted reward function only for a restrictive set of policies. It seems that the requirement of having $w_m < e^2 - 1$ makes this bound only tighter for policies very close to the logging policy in action probabilities. Please elaborate on why Proposition 1 is a significant result. 

-Unbiasedness of KL divergence estimators is shown to hold only asymptotically.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
-Isn't it better to call this setup 'missing-rewards' rather than 'unknown-rewards'.

-It is not clear why the logging policy is unknown. There is access to the propensity scores, which means that the logging policy is partially known. 

-The connection between the lower bound in Proposition 4 and the upper bounds in Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 is not clear. Please elaborate on the tightness of these bounds. 

-Why not compute (10) and (11) by averaging over all data instances in the union of $S$ and $S_u$?

-Experiments demonstrate that the performance of the proposed method depends on the quality of the logging policy. The improvement achieved by the algorithms over the logging policy is small. What will happen when the logging policy is just recommending actions uniformly at random? Will your policies still perform slightly better than the logging policy?
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper tackles the problem of CRM with missing rewards. The problem itself is interesting, and the proposed algorithms partially address it. However, the current version of the paper raises questions about the optimality of the proposed methods. The tightness of the theoretical bounds, improvements that the new algorithms achieve over the state-of-the-art, and dependence of the results on knowledge of propensity scores are some of the main issues that require further treatment.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies offline contextual bandit in the setting where the reward for some samples are not observed thus it is necessary to leverage the reward-free logged data to improve the performance of offline contextual bandits. The paper draws a connection to semi-supervised learning and propose two methods: (i) regularizing the policy to the behavior policy in the reward-free data, and (ii) predicting the rewards of reward-free samples and then augment them into the training data. Their algorithms require the knowledge of the behavior policy and the propensity scores. In their experiments with FashionMNISt and CIFAR-10, they show that leveraging the reward-free data with their methods at proper hyperparameter can improve over BanditNet that ignores the model-free data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**: 

- The problem of offline contextual bandit with reward-free data is practically relevant and can encourage more research in this direction. 

- The title is attractive

**Weaknesses** 

- Though the title is attractive, what the paper offers do not live up to this title. I thought there would be some analysis between neural representation with semi-supervised learning for offline contextual bandit but the paper simply employed neural net to train on the data and the proposed methods are even questionable (see below)

- The assumption to have access to pi_0 and know the propensity score is very strong which significantly limits the scope of this work. 

- experiments are too simple to suggest any useful conclusion: (i) only one setting: 90% of unlabeled data + 10% labeled data and (ii) only 3 methods: KL-CRM, WCE-CRM, PR-CRM. It would be better to show the results for other data split and include more competitive baselines. 

- What I am really concerned about is if regularizing pi wrt pi0 on the unlabeled data is a good way to leverage unlabeled data. The paper should clearly demonstrate if there is a benefit to policy regularization in unlabeled data. Plainly showing the expected risk cannot show that benefit. For example, if we use any of these methods (loss + policy reg term) but do not use unlabeled data (i.e. perform policy regularization in the labeled data instead of unlabeled data), how the performance would be? If it has a comparable performance with the same methods but trained reg term on unlabeled data, the performance gain is simply from policy regularization, not from unlabeled data.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- why write two eqs 15 and 16? when they are similar?
- either expected risk or accuracy would be enough, do not need to show both
- Figures are small and minimal

- it’s unclear what is $t_g$
content.summary_of_the_review: See the strength and weaknesses section.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
